questions.explanation: A service relationship is the ongoing cooperation made up of service provision (the monthly patching and support), service consumption, and relationship management (the quarterly review). The published tiers are the service offering, which describes what is available before any relationship exists, and the manufacturer's warranty belongs to a separate supplier arrangement outside the MSP-client relationship.

questions.question: A team comparing two backup vendors lists four considerations. Which two are risks in ITIL's sense, rather than costs? (Choose two.)
options: The cheaper vendor has suffered two multi-day outages this year
The premium vendor charges 40% more per terabyte stored
Choosing the cheaper vendor means forgoing an integration that would let the team retire a legacy tool
Migration will consume about 80 hours of staff time whichever vendor is chosen
questions.explanation: A risk is a possible event that could cause harm or make objectives harder to reach, which covers the outage history and also the missed opportunity to retire the legacy tool, since ITIL explicitly counts lost opportunities as risk. The price premium and the migration effort are costs: resources spent on a specific activity. The missed-integration option is the one candidates most often misfile as a cost.

questions.question: A hospital uses a scheduling application licensed from a software company and pays an MSP to configure, run, and support it. Which two statements are correct? (Choose two.)
options: The MSP is the service provider to the hospital
The software company is the hospital's service provider, since it owns the product
The hospital is the service consumer, with customer, user, and sponsor roles possibly spread across different staff
The software company cannot be a digital product vendor, because its product is used inside a service relationship
questions.explanation: The provider is whoever is in the service relationship delivering the service, which is the MSP; the hospital is the consumer, and its staff can hold the customer, user, and sponsor roles in any combination. Owning the product does not make the software company the provider: supplying a product without a service relationship to the hospital is exactly what a digital product vendor does, and that status is unaffected by someone else building a service on top of the product.

questions.question: A team drafts four 'working agreements'. Which two restate an ITIL guiding principle, rather than something ITIL does not actually recommend? (Choose two.)
options: Ship small changes and review how each one landed before starting the next
Remove manual effort only after the process it supports has been streamlined
Standardize every team on one process before any improvement work begins
Build each new service from a clean slate to avoid inheriting legacy problems
questions.explanation: The first is progress iteratively with feedback and the second is optimize and automate in its correct order. Standardizing before improving is not a principle and conflicts with keep it simple and practical, and starting from a clean slate is the opposite of start where you are, which asks teams to assess and reuse what already exists.

questions.question: Which two of the following situations are failures of think and work holistically, rather than of collaborate and promote visibility? (Choose two.)
options: A network change passes testing but silently breaks a finance report that relied on the old route
An SLA is agreed for one service without noticing it depends on a supplier whose own targets are looser
Two teams investigate the same outage because neither can see the other's queue
A project's risk register is kept in a private spreadsheet until the monthly steering meeting
questions.explanation: The first two are missed dependencies: a change or a commitment made without seeing how it connects to the rest of the system, which is what think and work holistically guards against. The other two are hidden work and hidden information, which is the domain of collaborate and promote visibility. Both principles concern openness, but one is about understanding connections and the other about sharing what is happening.

questions.question: Which two statements correctly describe how ITIL's management practices are organized and used? (Choose two.)
options: The 34 practices divide into general management practices and product and service management practices
A single practice can contribute to many different value streams
Each practice maps to exactly one lifecycle activity
Technical management practices form a third, separate group in the current model
questions.explanation: The current model groups the 34 practices into 12 general management and 22 product and service management practices, and any practice, incident management for instance, can be drawn into whichever value streams need it. Practices are not tied to a single lifecycle activity, and the separate technical management group from older material no longer exists.

questions.question: A team's improvement write-up contains four statements. Which two correspond to a step of the Continual Improvement Model? (Choose two.)
options: 'Average resolution time is currently 9.5 hours, measured over the last quarter'
'We will track the new figure monthly and revisit the target in six months'
'The vendor has agreed a 10% discount on the new tooling'
'The change advisory board met twice this month'
questions.explanation: The measured baseline is 'where are we now?' and the plan to keep tracking and revisiting is 'how do we keep the momentum going?'. A vendor discount and a board meeting are ordinary project events; neither is a step of the model, whose seven steps run from 'what is the vision?' through to sustaining momentum.

questions.question: A consultant maps parts of an organization onto the ITIL Value System. Which two mappings are correct? (Choose two.)
options: The board's policy that every change needs a documented risk assessment: governance
The incident management team with its tooling and procedures: management practices
The 'resolve an incident' flow from first report to closure: the value chain
The four-dimensions checklist used in design reviews: continual improvement
questions.explanation: A leadership mandate is governance, and a team with its tools and procedures organized for one kind of work is a management practice. The incident flow is a value stream built from value chain activities, not the value chain itself, which is the near-miss. The four dimensions are a separate model and are not a Value System component at all.

questions.question: A post-incident review lists four contributing causes. Which two belong to the organizations and people dimension? (Choose two.)
options: The on-call engineer had never been trained on the new storage platform
Nobody was clearly accountable for approving the vendor's emergency patch
The monitoring tool's alert threshold had been set too high to fire
The hosting contract gave the vendor 24 hours to respond to critical issues
questions.explanation: Skills and clear accountability are both organizations and people matters. The alert threshold is a configuration issue in information and technology, and the contractual response time sits in partners and suppliers. The accountability gap is the near-miss because a vendor is involved, but the missing piece is an internal role, not the contract.

questions.question: A project plan lists four work packages. Which two sit in the Transition activity of the Product and Service Lifecycle? (Choose two.)
options: Running user-acceptance testing against the assembled solution
Releasing the solution to the first wave of branch offices
Writing the interface specification the supplier must meet
Handling the first month of user-reported defects after go-live
questions.explanation: Transition covers moving a new or changed service into live use, which includes testing and release. The interface specification is Design work, and dealing with defects reported by users once live is Support. The defects option is the near-miss: it follows release closely, but by then the service is in use and the activity has moved on.

questions.question: Which two statements about a 'resolve a customer incident' value stream are correct? (Choose two.)
options: It may draw on several practices, such as service desk, incident management, and change enablement
It is complete when the customer confirms service is restored and they can work again
It must pass through all eight lifecycle activities to qualify as a value stream
It is complete as soon as the technician applies the fix, whatever the customer then experiences
questions.explanation: A value stream strings together whichever practices and lifecycle activities one scenario needs, and it ends when the consumer actually realizes value, not when an internal step finishes. Few value streams touch all eight activities, and the technician-applies-the-fix option is the near-miss: it describes an output being produced, not the outcome that closes the stream.

questions.question: Which two of the following AI uses are correctly matched to their capability in the AI Capability Model? (Choose two.)
options: A virtual agent that chats with users to gather incident details: Communication
An orchestrator that sequences the diagnostic, approval, and remediation steps across tools: Coordination
A model that ranks which open incidents are likely to breach their targets: Curation
A tool that condenses a 30-page vendor contract into its key obligations: Cognition
questions.explanation: Interacting with people is Communication and orchestrating a workflow across tools is Coordination. Ranking incidents by likely breach is a prediction, which is Cognition rather than Curation, and condensing a contract into plain key points is Clarification (or Curation of its content), not Cognition. The six capabilities are Creation, Curation, Clarification, Cognition, Communication, and Coordination.

questions.question: A company sells a SaaS platform (the software itself) and separately provides onboarding and support to help clients get value from it. Which is the digital product, and which is the digital service?
options: The SaaS platform is the digital service; onboarding and support is the digital product
Both onboarding and the platform are considered digital products
The SaaS platform is the digital product; onboarding and support constitute the digital service
Both are digital services, since the client pays for them under one subscription
questions.explanation: The platform itself, existing primarily in digital form, is the digital product. The value co-created through using it, including the onboarding and support that help a client get outcomes from it, is the digital service. Calling the platform the service and the onboarding the product swaps the two, calling both products collapses the difference between what is delivered and the value it enables, and how the client is billed does not change which part is the product.

questions.question: A new service manager asks what the value chain component actually is, given that her team already has practices and value streams. Which answer is correct?
options: The master list of all 34 practices and which team owns each one
The single value stream that handles the organization's most important service
The set of policies through which leadership directs the practices
The operating model of activities that value streams draw on to turn demand into value
questions.explanation: The value chain is an operating model, expressed as the eight lifecycle activities, from which every value stream selects the activities a scenario needs. The practice list is the management practices component, a single flow is one value stream rather than the chain they all draw on, and policies from leadership are governance.

questions.question: A government passes a data-residency law; a currency slump makes overseas hosting 30% more expensive; and public pressure is growing over how companies use customer data. Which option labels these three PESTLE factors in order?
options: Legal, Economic, Social
Political, Economic, Social
Legal, Technological, Political
Political, Legal, Social
questions.explanation: An enacted law creating a compliance requirement is Legal, a currency movement is Economic, and shifting public attitudes are Social. Political is the near-miss for the first item, but Political covers government stability and policy direction, whereas a law already in force is Legal. Nothing in the scenario describes a technology trend.

questions.question: A payroll service is live. Which of the following is an example of the Deliver activity, as distinct from Operate, Support, or Transition?
options: The platform team running the overnight payroll batch and monitoring it
Employees receiving correct payslips on the agreed date each month
The desk correcting a payslip an employee reports as wrong
The release team cutting over to the new payroll version
questions.explanation: Deliver is the consumer actually receiving the agreed outcome, which is the payslip arriving correctly and on time. Running and monitoring the batch is Operate, fixing a reported error is Support, and the version cut-over is Transition. The batch run is the near-miss because it produces the payslips, but it is the internal running of the service rather than the outcome reaching the consumer.

questions.question: An MSP's procurement team runs a stream that renews and re-assigns the software licences its support engineers depend on. A new manager wants it reclassified as core, arguing that 'without it, client support would stop'. Which statement is correct?
options: It stays enabling: it supports other value streams but serves no external customer directly
It becomes core: any stream that core work depends on inherits core status from them
It is neither: licence handling is a management practice rather than a value stream
It becomes core: the licences are ultimately paid for out of external client fees
questions.explanation: Core versus enabling is decided by whether the stream creates value directly for an external customer, not by how critical it is or who ultimately funds it. Dependency does not transfer core status, and an end-to-end renewal flow spanning several steps and practices is a value stream, not a single practice.

questions.question: A CIO learns that ITIL, Agile, DevOps, and PRINCE2 are all 'in use' across her organization and worries they conflict. Which statement best explains how they can coexist?
options: ITIL supplies the service value system and governance; the others contribute practices for how particular work gets done
Each covers the full service lifecycle, so the organization should standardize on whichever is most mature
ITIL incorporates the other three, so adopting ITIL means the others are already in place
The others apply only to development work, while ITIL applies only to live operations
questions.explanation: The frameworks sit at different layers: ITIL frames the overall value system, while Agile, DevOps, and PRINCE2 offer specific ways of doing iterative, delivery, and project work inside it. The claim that the others apply only to development while ITIL applies only to live operations is the near-miss, since ITIL also covers Discover, Design, and Build rather than operations alone. ITIL neither absorbs the others nor demands a single-framework choice.

questions.question: A software company that only licenses a product to an organization, with no provision, consumption, or relationship-management activities between them, is still that organization's service provider because it owns the product.
questions.explanation: Owning the product does not create a service relationship. With none of the relationship activities present, the company is a digital product vendor; the service provider is whoever is actually in the service relationship with the organization, which may be an MSP running the product on its behalf, or the organization's own IT team.

questions.question: After an AI triage assistant is introduced, deciding who may override its recommendations and who is accountable when it is wrong belongs to the organizations and people dimension.
questions.explanation: Roles, responsibilities, and accountability are organizations and people matters, and the current model explicitly extends that dimension to the skills and oversight duties AI creates. The assistant itself sits in information and technology, which is why candidates often misfile the accountability question there too.

questions.question: A team that has completed the Design activity has, by definition, already placed the orders for the components the design calls for.
questions.explanation: Design produces requirements and specifications; obtaining components from suppliers is Acquire, the activity that follows. The boundary matters because a specification can still change cheaply, whereas a placed order commits money and supplier time.

questions.question: A DevOps team that deploys through an automated pipeline is operating outside ITIL change enablement, because ITIL requires every change to be individually approved.
questions.explanation: Change enablement classifies changes by risk: a low-risk, well-understood, pre-authorized change is a standard change and needs no case-by-case approval, which is exactly how a tested pipeline deployment can be governed. DevOps practices sit inside the ITIL value system rather than outside it.

questions.question: In a managed-service contract, the client's CFO funds it, its IT director sets the requirements, and its 400 staff raise the tickets. The MSP's account manager keeps referring to 'the consumer'. Who is she referring to?
options: The client organization as a whole, across all three roles
Only the 400 staff, since they consume the service day to day
Only the IT director, since the consumer is whoever defines requirements
The MSP itself, since it consumes the client's budget
questions.explanation: The consumer is the party receiving the service, and that party can hold the sponsor, customer, and user roles across different people. Narrowing it to the staff confuses consumer with user, narrowing it to the director confuses consumer with customer, and the MSP is the provider, not the consumer.

questions.question: A team chooses a cheaper hosting provider with a weaker outage track record, planning to accept the occasional downtime instead of paying for a premium, more reliable option. What trade-off does this decision represent?
options: Lower cost accepted in exchange for higher risk
Lower risk accepted in exchange for higher cost
Lower utility accepted in exchange for higher warranty
Lower warranty accepted in exchange for higher utility
questions.explanation: Cost and risk trade off against each other -- spending less here means accepting a greater chance of a costly outage. Utility and warranty describe the service's own functional and reliability qualities, not a financial choice between hosting providers, so framing this specific trade-off in those terms swaps in the wrong pair of concepts.

questions.question: A managed print contract lists two printer models, a monthly ticket allowance, and a 4-hour response time. Six months in, the account manager is also running renewal conversations and adjusting the ticket allowance to actual usage. Which term captures that ongoing account work specifically, as opposed to what the contract lists?
options: The service relationship
The service offering
A management practice
The digital product vendor role
questions.explanation: The contract's fixed list of printers, tickets, and response times is the service offering. The renewal conversations and usage-based adjustments are relationship management activities, which together with provision and consumption make up the service relationship. 'Account management' is not one of ITIL's 34 named practices, and supplying hardware does not make this a vendor-only arrangement when ongoing support commitments are part of the deal.

questions.question: A support team holds a daily 10-minute standup where they openly share which incidents are open, blocked, or at risk, so other departments can see the current state without having to ask. Which guiding principle is this most directly an example of?
options: Collaborate and promote visibility
Think and work holistically
Progress iteratively with feedback
Optimize and automate
questions.explanation: Openly sharing current status so others can see what's happening without asking is exactly collaborate and promote visibility. It isn't specifically about ripple effects across the organization (think and work holistically), incremental delivery (progress iteratively with feedback), or reducing manual effort (optimize and automate).

questions.question: Leadership sets a policy requiring every improvement initiative to report progress against a documented baseline before it can move on to planning how it will get there. Which two Value System concepts does this combine?
options: Governance and the Continual Improvement Model
Two guiding principles applied together
The value chain and a value stream
Management practices and the four dimensions
questions.explanation: Leadership mandating a rule is governance directing and controlling how work happens, and the baseline-before-plan sequence it enforces is the Continual Improvement Model's 'where are we now?' and 'how do we get there?' steps. No guiding principle mandates anything, the value chain and value streams describe how work flows rather than policy, and the four dimensions are not a Value System component.

questions.question: A team wants to reduce the seven manual fields analysts fill out when closing a ticket. Three of those fields duplicate data already captured elsewhere in the ticketing system. Their first move is to build a bot that auto-fills all seven fields exactly as analysts currently type them, including the three duplicates. What did the team get wrong?
options: They automated before simplifying, so the redundant fields are now built into the bot
Nothing; automating first reveals which fields can be simplified later
They applied the wrong principle; field counts are governed by focus on value, not optimize and automate
They breached start where you are by changing the analysts' manual process at all
questions.explanation: Optimize and automate calls for simplifying first and automating what remains; automating with the three duplicate fields still in place makes the redundancy run faster and harder to remove. Automating first and simplifying later has the order reversed, focus on value does not govern step reduction the way keep it simple and practical does, and start where you are means assessing what exists, not refusing to change it.

questions.question: After acquiring a smaller IT provider, a company must integrate the acquired firm's outsourced backup-monitoring vendor into its own workflows, redesigning how a backup-failure alert gets routed and escalated. Which two dimensions does this integration touch most directly?
options: Partners and suppliers, and value streams and processes
Partners and suppliers, and information and technology
Organizations and people, and value streams and processes
Information and technology, and organizations and people
questions.explanation: The outsourced vendor relationship sits under partners and suppliers, and redesigning how an alert is routed and escalated is a workflow change under value streams and processes. Information and technology is the tempting near-miss because backups are technical, but the scenario describes no tooling change, and no retraining or role change is mentioned for organizations and people.

questions.question: A team has already piloted a new expense-reporting tool with one department and is now making it available to all employees, after which the platform team will keep it running day to day. Which two lifecycle activities are happening here, in order?
options: Transition, then Operate
Transition, then Support
Design, then Build
Discover, then Deliver
questions.explanation: Moving from a limited pilot into full live availability is Transition, and running the tool day to day afterward is Operate. Support would instead mean resolving issues and requests rather than routine day-to-day running, and Design/Build or Discover/Deliver describe earlier or different activities than what's happening in this scenario.

questions.question: Which of the following is the best example of an enabling value stream?
options: Renewing an internal software license used only by the IT department itself
Resolving a customer-facing support ticket
Delivering a signed contract directly to an external client
Responding to a customer's product inquiry
questions.explanation: Renewing an internal license never touches the external customer directly, which is exactly what makes it an enabling value stream -- it supports other value streams internally instead. Resolving a ticket, delivering a contract, and responding to an inquiry all involve direct interaction with an external customer, making each of those a core value stream instead.

questions.question: A provider adds a costly redundant failover system, and customers still consider the service worth paying for afterward because outages are now rare. What term describes that overall perceived worth, weighing the added cost against the reduced risk?
options: Warranty
Value
Output
Outcome
questions.explanation: Value is the perceived worth a stakeholder assigns once utility and warranty are weighed against cost and risk, which is the judgement the customers are making. Warranty is only the improved availability itself, the failover system is an output, and rare outages are the outcome; the question asks about the overall weighing of that outcome against the added cost.

questions.question: Buying an ITSM tool suite with incident, request, and change modules gives an organization service management capability, since the tool supplies the processes.
questions.explanation: Service management is a set of organizational capabilities spanning people, process, information, and technology working together. A tool is one technology input; without skilled people, agreed processes, and reliable information the capability does not exist, which is why tool purchases alone so often fail to improve service.

questions.question: A team documents clear, structured steps for logging and routing a ticket, but has no defined people, tools, or other resources organized around those steps yet. What's missing to call this a full management practice rather than just a process?
options: Nothing; a process and a practice are the same thing
The people, tools, and other resources organized around the steps
A governance decision authorizing the steps
A value stream for the steps to belong to
questions.explanation: A practice is the broader bundle: people, tools, information, and other resources organized around one or more processes to accomplish an objective; a process alone is just the structured set of activities. Governance authorization is not what turns a process into a practice, and a value stream is a separate construct that would use the practice rather than complete it.

questions.question: A hospital's patient-portal service is under review. Which two of the following are stakeholders in the service even though none of them is its customer, user, or sponsor? (Choose two.)
options: The health regulator that audits how patient data is handled
The hospital's internal auditor assessing the portal's access controls
The nurse who logs in each shift to update patient records
The operations director who signed off the portal's budget
questions.explanation: A stakeholder is anyone with an interest in or expectations of an activity or decision, so the regulator and the internal auditor qualify without using, funding, or specifying the service. The nurse is a user and the operations director is the sponsor: both are stakeholders too, but they hold one of the three named roles, which the question excludes.

questions.question: A shareholder who has never used the company's online-banking service, and is neither its customer nor its sponsor, cannot be a stakeholder in that service.
questions.explanation: Stakeholder requires only an interest in or expectations of an activity or decision. A shareholder has a clear interest in whether the service protects revenue and reputation, so they qualify without holding any of the customer, user, or sponsor roles, just as a regulator or auditor would.

questions.question: A migration project is broken into quarterly releases, with each one adjusted based on what users report after the previous release goes live. Which guiding principle does this best demonstrate?
options: Think and work holistically
Progress iteratively with feedback
Optimize and automate
Start where you are
questions.explanation: Breaking work into smaller pieces, checking it against real feedback, and adjusting before the next piece is exactly progress iteratively with feedback.

questions.question: Before a database upgrade, a project manager publishes the change plan on a shared board, invites support, finance, and security to comment, and posts daily progress so anyone can see where it stands. Which guiding principle is most directly illustrated?
options: Collaborate and promote visibility
Think and work holistically
Progress iteratively with feedback
Keep it simple and practical
questions.explanation: Opening the plan to other teams, inviting their input, and making progress visible is collaborate and promote visibility. Think and work holistically is the near-miss: it would be the better fit if the scenario emphasized analysing how the upgrade affects downstream systems, but what is described is openness and involvement. No incremental delivery or step reduction is mentioned.

questions.question: Think and work holistically is satisfied when a team makes its change plan visible to other teams, even if nobody checks how the change will affect their systems.
questions.explanation: Making the plan visible is collaborate and promote visibility. Think and work holistically requires actually understanding how the change connects to and affects other parts of the organization; publishing a plan nobody analyses for impact leaves exactly the downstream breakage the principle exists to prevent.

questions.question: A service desk wants to automate ticket categorization. Which two actions are consistent with the guiding principle optimize and automate? (Choose two.)
options: First merging the 40 overlapping categories into the 12 analysts actually use
Measuring how often current categories get corrected later, before deciding what to automate
Automating all 40 existing categories as they are, so the model can learn which are redundant
Leaving categorization manual, since the principle applies only when a whole process is replaced
questions.explanation: The principle is to understand and streamline a process first, then automate what remains, so consolidating the categories and measuring the current error rate both come before any automation. Automating the 40 categories as-is bakes the redundancy into the model, and the principle applies to any work where human effort can be reduced, not only wholesale replacement of a manual process.

questions.question: Leadership mandates that every production change must include a documented rollback plan. The team that actually writes and tests each specific rollback plan is performing:
options: Governance
A management practice
A guiding principle
Continual improvement
questions.explanation: Leadership's mandate is governance, directing and controlling from the top; the team that writes and tests each rollback plan is carrying the mandate out with organizational resources, which is a management practice (change enablement). Governance is the near-miss because the rule came from leadership, but the question asks about the team doing the work. No guiding principle produces a plan, and continual improvement would describe reviewing and refining the rule over time.

questions.question: A change manager who assesses, authorizes, and schedules each normal change is performing governance, because authorizing changes is a form of control.
questions.explanation: Governance is the governing body evaluating, directing, and monitoring the organization as a whole, for example mandating that every change be risk-assessed. Assessing and authorizing individual changes under that mandate is the change enablement practice at work: a management practice carrying out the direction, not the direction itself.

questions.question: A routine password reset request passes through four separate approval systems before completion, even though staffing, tools, and vendor relationships are all fine. Which dimension does this problem sit in?
options: Organizations and people
Value streams and processes
Partners and suppliers
Information and technology
questions.explanation: Unnecessary steps and handoffs in how a request actually moves are a value streams and processes problem, not a staffing, tooling, or vendor issue.

questions.question: A company moves its hardware-support contract to a new supplier whose engineers now attend site, and makes one of its own analysts the supplier's named point of contact with a new set of responsibilities. The tooling and the request workflow are unchanged. Which two dimensions does this touch most directly? (Choose two.)
options: Partners and suppliers
Organizations and people
Information and technology
Value streams and processes
questions.explanation: A new supplier relationship sits under partners and suppliers, and a changed role with new responsibilities for an in-house analyst sits under organizations and people. The scenario explicitly rules out a tooling change (information and technology) and a workflow change (value streams and processes), which is what makes the other two options distractors rather than extra answers.

questions.question: A team is in the Build activity when testing reveals the original requirements were incomplete. What should happen next, given how the Product and Service Lifecycle is meant to work?
options: Keep building and fix the requirements later during Support
Loop back to Design to address the gap before continuing
Restart the lifecycle from Discover, since the model runs one way
Move on to Transition and record the gap as a known error
questions.explanation: The lifecycle is iterative by design, so returning to Design when Build exposes a requirements gap is the expected move, not a failure. Deferring the fix to Support ships a known gap to users, restarting from Discover throws away valid work and misreads the model as linear, and a known error is a problem-management record for a live fault, not a way to carry an unresolved requirement into release.

questions.question: Which of the following describes a value stream, rather than work inside a single management practice?
options: Logging and categorizing a reported fault at the service desk
Resolving a user's incident from first report to confirmed closure
Assessing and authorizing a normal change at the change advisory board
Diagnosing a suspected network fault within the network team
questions.explanation: A value stream runs end to end for one scenario, from demand to value realized, and typically crosses several practices on the way: here the service desk, incident management, possibly change enablement, and the user confirming the outcome. The other three are each a step inside one practice (service desk, change enablement, incident management), however important that step is.

questions.question: In a 'fulfil an access request' value stream, the stream is finished once the access team has provisioned the account, even if the user has not yet been told how to log in.
questions.explanation: A value stream ends when the consumer actually realizes value, which here means the user can log in and work. Provisioning is an internal step producing an output; until the user knows about it and can use it, the outcome has not occurred and the stream is still open, however complete the internal work looks.

questions.question: Which two of the following describe a value stream, rather than a single practice or a single step within one? (Choose two.)
options: Taking a new starter from signed offer to a productive first day with laptop, badge, and access
Taking a feature from customer request through build, release, and first use
Change enablement, including its risk-assessment and authorization steps
The approval step in which the change authority signs off a normal change
questions.explanation: The first two run end to end from a demand to value realized by the consumer, drawing on several practices along the way, which is what a value stream is. Change enablement is a single practice, however many steps it contains, and the authorization step is one activity inside that practice. The practice option is the near-miss: it has internal steps, but it is still one set of resources for one kind of work.

lessons.title: The Language of Value: Products, Services & Outcomes
lessons.summary: The precise vocabulary ITIL uses to separate what a provider delivers from what actually satisfies the customer.
lessons.reading:
ITIL draws a careful line between a product and a service. A product, in ITIL's terms, is a configuration of an organization's resources — the actual thing that exists, like a piece of software or a support contract. A service is what that product enables: value co-created with the customer by facilitating the outcomes they actually want, without the customer having to manage the underlying costs and risks themselves. The same distinction carries over to digital work specifically: a digital product is something that exists primarily in digital form — an app, a dataset, a SaaS platform — while the digital service is the value realized through using it, including everything from onboarding to ongoing support.

That same "what you get" versus "what it does for you" split shows up again in output versus outcome. An output is a tangible or intangible deliverable of some activity — a closed ticket, a deployed patch, a generated report. An outcome is the actual result that output makes possible for a stakeholder — the user working uninterrupted again, the business staying compliant. ITIL consistently steers attention toward outcomes, because counting outputs, like tickets closed or patches deployed, can look productive while missing whether anything real actually improved for the person on the other end.

Within a service itself, utility and warranty describe two different qualities. Utility is what the service does — its functionality, whether it removes a constraint or supports a performance need — commonly summarized as "fit for purpose." Warranty is how well and reliably it does it: availability, capacity, security, and continuity, or "fit for use." A service that's functionally perfect but constantly down has utility without warranty, and a service that never goes down but doesn't do what's needed has warranty without utility — value needs both. That warranty dimension gets formalized further through service level and SLA: a service level is one measured performance target, and an SLA is the documented agreement that records one or more of those targets along with what happens if they're missed.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to this kind of vocabulary? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Think about buying a car versus what owning one actually gets you. The car itself — the metal, the engine, the software running it — is the product. What that car actually gives you, getting to work reliably every day without you having to be a mechanic yourself, is the service. Utility is whether the car does what you need, like whether it fits five passengers or gets good mileage; warranty is whether it's reliable enough to depend on, like whether it starts every morning or is covered if something breaks. And the odometer reading after a road trip is an output, a number produced by the drive, while actually arriving somewhere you needed to be is the outcome that made the drive worth taking.
commonTraps: Utility is not the same as quality overall — it's specifically the functional 'what,' not reliability.
An output isn't automatically valuable just because it was produced — the outcome is what determines whether it mattered.
A service level and an SLA are not interchangeable terms: the level is the target, the SLA is the agreement that documents it.
Warranty covers more than uptime alone — capacity, security, and continuity all count too.
lessons.scenario: A managed service provider proudly reports that its help desk closed 500 tickets last month — an output. But when a client's finance team is asked whether things actually feel better, they mention that recurring printer failures still interrupt their workday weekly, just with faster tickets each time. The provider optimized for output volume while the outcome the client actually needed, uninterrupted printing, never improved. A revised SLA that tracks repeat-incident rate, not just closure speed, would better capture the warranty and outcome the client is actually paying for.
lessons.onTheJob: In a real service desk, 'ticket volume' and 'first-response time' are exactly the output metrics that end up on a manager's dashboard because they're easy to count, even when everyone privately knows they don't reflect whether users are actually less frustrated — pushing a team to report on outcome measures like repeat-incident rate is usually an uphill argument, not a given. SLA negotiations in practice are also as much about which warranty dimension actually gets measured, uptime versus response time versus how a breach gets remediated, as about the headline percentage everyone fixates on first. A common misconfiguration is writing an SLA that only credits downtime against an uptime figure while leaving capacity or security failures out of the document entirely, which quietly narrows warranty down to just one of its four components until an incident falls outside what the contract actually covers.

lessons.title: Roles, Relationships & Value Streams
lessons.summary: Who is who in a service relationship, how cost and risk trade off, and what separates a core value stream from an enabling one.
lessons.reading:
ITIL separates the people involved in a service relationship into distinct roles, and more than one role can land on the same person. The customer defines requirements and is accountable for the outcomes the service produces. The user is whoever actually consumes the service day to day. The sponsor is whoever authorizes the budget that pays for it. A single department head might be customer, user, and sponsor all at once, or those roles might be split across three completely different people — the exam expects you to identify which role a scenario is actually describing, not assume they're always the same person.

On the provider side of the relationship, the provider is whoever delivers the service, and the consumer is whoever receives it, as customer, user, sponsor, or some combination. A digital product vendor sits slightly outside this: it supplies a product, like a licensed piece of software, without necessarily being in an ongoing service relationship with whoever uses it. That relationship itself, once it exists, is called the service relationship — the whole cooperation between provider and consumer covering service provision, service consumption, and the relationship management activities that keep it running, not just the moment of delivery. What's actually on offer in the first place is the service offering: the goods, resource access, and service actions bundled together for a specific consumer group, like the tiers of a support plan.

Two more distinctions round this category out. Cost is simply the money spent on a specific activity or resource, while risk is broader: a possible event that could cause harm or make objectives harder to reach, including a missed opportunity, not only a downside. The two often trade off against each other, and exam scenarios frequently ask you to weigh a cheaper option against the risk it introduces. Separately, a core value stream is one that creates value directly for an external customer, while an enabling value stream supports other value streams internally, like renewing a supplier contract, without ever touching that external customer directly.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to service roles? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Picture a family cell phone plan. The parent who signs the contract and pays the bill is the sponsor. Whichever family member decided the plan needed unlimited data because everyone streams video is the customer. The teenager actually using the phone every day is the user — and none of that requires three different people; the parent could easily be sponsor, customer, and a user all at once. The phone manufacturer, meanwhile, sold a device but has no ongoing relationship with the family managing their plan — that's the digital product vendor. And choosing the cheapest carrier over a slightly pricier one with better coverage is a cost-versus-risk trade-off in miniature: less spent now, but more risk of dropped calls later.
commonTraps: Customer, user, and sponsor are distinct roles, but nothing stops one person from holding all three at once.
A digital product vendor is not automatically the service provider — supplying a product does not require an ongoing service relationship.
Risk isn't limited to financial loss, and it includes missed opportunities, not just downside events.
An enabling value stream still matters even though it never touches the external customer directly — it's what makes core value streams possible.
lessons.scenario: An IT consultancy sells a monitoring dashboard license outright to a client, with no support contract attached — that's a digital product vendor relationship, not a full service relationship. Separately, the same consultancy runs a managed help desk for another client, where the client's operations director approved the contract (sponsor), the client's IT manager defined the requirements (customer), and frontline staff log tickets daily (users). Internally, the consultancy's own supplier-renewal process for its ticketing software license is an enabling value stream — it never touches either client directly, but without it, the core value stream of actually resolving client tickets would eventually break down.
lessons.onTheJob: Figuring out who the real 'customer' is on a support ticket matters in practice because escalations get routed differently depending on whether you're arguing with the day-to-day user or the budget-holding sponsor — a frustrated user complaining loudly is not always who has the authority to approve a fix that costs money. Enabling value streams, like renewing a monitoring tool's license, are also the first thing that gets deprioritized when a team is busy, right up until the license lapses and takes down the core value stream it was quietly supporting.

lessons.title: The ITIL Value System & Guiding Principles
lessons.summary: The five components that make up the Value System, and the seven guiding principles that steer decisions everywhere.
lessons.reading:
The ITIL Service Value System is the overall model tying everything else in the framework together, and it has exactly five components: guiding principles, governance, the service value chain, management practices, and continual improvement. Guiding principles are recommendations meant to guide an organization in every circumstance, regardless of what's changing around it — they're deliberately generic so they apply whether you're troubleshooting one ticket or restructuring an entire department. Management practices are the "how": organizational resources, people, process, and tools, assembled to actually perform value chain activities. In the current model, the 34 total practices split into 12 general management practices and 22 product and service management practices, with no separate small technical-management group the way older models had.

There are seven guiding principles, and Foundation expects you to recognize each by name and apply it to a scenario, not just recite the list. Focus on value means tracing every activity back to some benefit for a stakeholder — if a task doesn't map to that, it's worth questioning whether it's worth doing. Start where you are means assessing and reusing what already exists rather than building from scratch by default, which is not the same as refusing to change anything. Keep it simple and practical means using the minimum number of steps needed and cutting anything that doesn't add value — exam scenarios describing redundant approval steps almost always point here.

The remaining four principles fill in the rest of the picture: progress iteratively with feedback favors small, adjustable steps over one giant rollout; collaborate and promote visibility means sharing information openly across boundaries so people can see what's happening; think and work holistically means recognizing how a change in one part of the organization ripples into others; and optimize and automate means improving a process manually first, then automating what's left, since automating a broken process just makes it fail faster. These principles frequently get tested in pairs where two sound similar but target different problems, so read each scenario for exactly what's being described, not just which keyword it echoes.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to the idea of guiding principles? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: A family's household rules work the same way guiding principles do. 'Clean up your own mess' applies whether you're talking about dishes, laundry, or a school project — it's generic enough to guide behavior in any situation, the same way ITIL's principles are meant to apply whether you're handling a single ticket or a company reorganization. And just like a family might have several rules that sound similar but aren't the same, 'don't leave a mess' and 'don't waste food' both sound like tidiness rules, but one is about cleanliness and the other is about not being wasteful — exactly the kind of distinction the exam expects between principles like 'think and work holistically' and 'collaborate and promote visibility.'
commonTraps: There are exactly seven guiding principles, not five, six, or nine — a common wrong-answer trap on the exam.
'Start where you are' does not mean never changing anything — it means assessing what exists honestly before deciding what to keep.
'Optimize and automate' means simplify first, automate second — automating a bad process just fails faster.
'Think and work holistically' and 'collaborate and promote visibility' are both about openness, but one is about seeing the whole picture and the other is about sharing information.
lessons.scenario: A change advisory board requires three separate sign-offs for every request, including for a routine, pre-approved standard change that's been run successfully a hundred times before. Removing the two unnecessary sign-offs and leaving the one that actually adds risk oversight is 'keep it simple and practical' in action. If the board then wants to automate that remaining approval step with a bot that checks a few fixed conditions, that's 'optimize and automate' — but only after the simplification happened first, not instead of it.
lessons.onTheJob: In practice, 'keep it simple and practical' is the principle a manager actually invokes out loud, usually while killing a redundant approval step someone else added years ago for reasons nobody remembers — it's the guiding principle with the most day-to-day teeth. 'Start where you are' gets misused constantly as an excuse to never modernize anything, which is precisely the misreading the framework warns against, so a good manager ends up re-explaining that assessing what exists is a starting point for change, not a reason to avoid it.

lessons.title: Governance, Continual Improvement & Key Practices
lessons.summary: How governance directs the organization, how the Continual Improvement Model drives change, and how a handful of core practices fit together.
lessons.reading:
Governance is the Value System component covering how an organization is directed and controlled — evaluating, directing, and monitoring performance and compliance from the top. It sits above day-to-day operations and above any single management practice: a company's leadership setting a policy that all IT changes require a documented risk assessment is governance, while the change enablement practice that actually carries that policy out day to day is a management practice, not governance itself. The value chain component of the Value System — an operating model outlining the key activities an organization undertakes to convert inputs like demand and opportunity into outputs of value — is what all of this ultimately serves; it's covered in depth in its own lesson as the eight-stage Product and Service Lifecycle, since that's the concrete form it takes today, not a separate six-activity list some older material still describes.

Continual improvement is the Value System component that keeps all of this from going stale — a recurring activity performed across every part of the organization, not a one-time project, to make sure performance keeps meeting stakeholder expectations over time. It's operationalized through the seven-step Continual Improvement Model: what is the vision, where are we now, where do we want to be, how do we get there, take action, did we get there, and how do we keep the momentum going. The steps are sequential and dependent on each other — you can't credibly set a target (step 3) without an honest baseline (step 2), and skipping straight to an action plan without measuring the current state is one of the most common exam scenarios describing where a team went wrong. Teams can loop back to an earlier step as understanding improves, but they can't meaningfully skip ahead.

A handful of management practices come up often enough on the exam to be worth knowing individually, even at Foundation level. Incident management restores service as fast as possible after an unplanned interruption or reduction in quality; problem management separately investigates the underlying cause of one or more incidents to prevent recurrence, sometimes producing a known error, a problem that's been analyzed but not yet permanently fixed, often with a documented workaround in the meantime. Change enablement classifies changes by risk and urgency: a standard change is pre-authorized and needs no case-by-case approval, a normal change goes through assessment and authorization first, and an emergency change is fast-tracked because it can't wait for the normal process. The service desk, finally, is the single agreed point of contact for users — its value is coordination and communication, logging and routing issues, even when the actual resolution happens somewhere else entirely.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to governance and continual improvement? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Governance is like a city council setting building codes, while continual improvement is like the ongoing inspections that keep every building meeting code as materials age and standards evolve — one sets the rule, the other keeps checking it's still being met. And the seven-step model is exactly how you'd plan a home renovation: you wouldn't order kitchen cabinets, take action, before measuring your current kitchen, where are we now, and deciding what you actually want it to look like, where do we want to be — skipping either step means the cabinets probably won't fit or won't be what you needed.
commonTraps: Restoring service fast (incident management) and finding the root cause (problem management) are deliberately separate practices, not one combined step.
The Continual Improvement Model's steps depend on each other in order — you can't set a credible target without first knowing your actual baseline.
A standard change still requires pre-authorization; it's not the same as 'no process at all,' just no case-by-case approval.
The service desk doesn't need to resolve every issue itself to be doing its job — coordination and communication are its real value.
lessons.scenario: After a spike in checkout failures on an e-commerce platform, the service desk logs the incidents and restores service by restarting a failed process, resolving the immediate incident within the hour. Problem management then investigates separately and finds a memory leak in a recent deployment, logging it as a known error with the workaround documented for the support team while a permanent code fix is scheduled through a normal change. Meanwhile, leadership's governance decision that every production deployment needs a rollback plan is what made that restart even possible in minutes rather than hours.
lessons.onTheJob: Incident and problem management get blurred together constantly on a real service desk because the same person often does both jobs back to back — restart the service, then separately dig into why it broke — and a manager's real job is making sure the root-cause investigation actually happens once the fire is out, since it's the step that gets skipped under pressure. Known errors with a documented workaround are also where a lot of technical debt quietly accumulates, since a workaround that's 'good enough' can sit unfixed for years once the pressure to permanently resolve it fades. This same documented, rollback-plan-first discipline around approving a production change is what CompTIA's Cloud+ certification tests directly under its own Change management process flashcard, just framed around cloud operations rather than ITIL's broader service value system.

lessons.title: The Four Dimensions of Service Management
lessons.summary: The four angles every service must be viewed from, and the external PESTLE factors that press on all of them.
lessons.reading:
ITIL's Four Dimensions are a checklist for viewing any service from every angle needed to keep it working end to end, rather than fixating on just one. Organizations and people covers roles, responsibilities, structure, culture, and staffing — whether a support team actually has the right skills and headcount for what it's being asked to do. Information and technology covers the information and knowledge needed to manage services, plus the technologies that support them, explicitly including AI, cloud, and automation in the current model.

Partners and suppliers covers relationships with other organizations involved in designing, developing, deploying, or supporting a service — and this ranges from a single software license purchased from a vendor all the way to a large, formal outsourcing arrangement; scale and formality don't change which dimension a relationship belongs to. Value streams and processes covers the actual activities, workflows, controls, and procedures an organization uses to achieve its objectives — the "how work actually flows" dimension.

All four dimensions sit inside a wider environment shaped by external PESTLE factors: Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Legal, and Environmental pressures the organization doesn't control but has to respond to. A new data-residency law is a Legal factor; a shift toward remote-work culture is Social. The exam's real focus, though, is less on memorizing PESTLE's letters and more on recognizing that the four dimensions constantly affect each other — a technology change, like rolling out AI-assisted triage, almost always has a knock-on effect in organizations and people, since staff need new skills to review and override it, and the current model explicitly folds that AI-related shift into the organizations and people dimension itself, not just information and technology.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to the four dimensions? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Think about opening a small restaurant. You need the right staff with the right skills (organizations and people), a working point-of-sale system and kitchen equipment (information and technology), a reliable produce supplier (partners and suppliers), and an actual efficient process for taking an order and getting food to the table (value streams and processes). Miss any one of the four, and the whole restaurant suffers even if the other three are perfect — a great chef with no functioning register, or a great supplier relationship with untrained waitstaff, both fail the customer just the same. A new minimum-wage law, a PESTLE factor, can force changes across more than one of those four dimensions at once.
commonTraps: PESTLE factors are external pressures on the four dimensions, not a fifth dimension themselves.
Partners and suppliers is not only about big formal outsourcing deals — a single software license counts too.
Organizations and people covers more than headcount — skills, culture, and role clarity matter just as much.
A change rarely stays inside one dimension — the exam often describes a ripple effect across two dimensions at once.
lessons.scenario: A logistics company outsources its network monitoring to a third-party provider (partners and suppliers), which requires its own staff to be retrained on how to interpret the vendor's alerts correctly (organizations and people). Around the same time, new environmental regulations (a PESTLE factor) push the company to consolidate data centers, forcing a redesign of how incident tickets get routed between the old and new infrastructure (value streams and processes) alongside the monitoring platform migration itself (information and technology). No single dimension captures the whole change — all four move together.
lessons.onTheJob: A manager doing a real post-incident review uses the four dimensions less as vocabulary to recite and more as a checklist to make sure a fix doesn't just patch the technology while ignoring that staff also need retraining or that a vendor contract needs revisiting — missing one of the four is usually how the same incident recurs six months later. PESTLE factors show up as boring compliance memos from legal or HR that nobody reads until a new regulation forces an unplanned redesign of a process that was working fine the day before. A frequent blind spot inside partners and suppliers is treating a signed contract as proof the dimension is covered, when the more common real-world failure is that nobody ever actually tested the vendor's promised failover process until the day it was needed and it didn't work as documented.

lessons.title: The Product & Service Lifecycle
lessons.summary: The eight iterative activities that convert demand into delivered value — ITIL's value chain in practice.
lessons.reading:
The service value chain component of the Value System is expressed as the Product and Service Lifecycle: eight activities — Discover, Design, Acquire, Build, Transition, Operate, Deliver, Support — that convert inputs like demand and opportunity into outputs of value. This isn't a second, separate model sitting alongside "the value chain"; it's the same operating model, just expressed as a concrete, nameable sequence of activities rather than an abstract concept. Crucially, it's used iteratively, not as a strict one-way pipeline: work can loop back to an earlier activity at any point, and that looping is expected, not a sign something went wrong.

The first four activities take a service from idea to built component. Discover means identifying opportunities and understanding demand — is there a real problem worth solving here, before anything gets designed. Design defines requirements and specifications, but nothing gets built or acquired yet at this stage; that boundary between defining what's needed and actually producing it is a distinction the exam tests directly. Acquire and Build both then produce the actual components a solution needs: Acquire obtains them from outside suppliers, Build develops them in house, and a single project often uses both at once.

The final four activities move that built solution into live use and keep it running. Transition covers moving a new or changed product or service into live use, including testing and release — this is where change management and deployment activity concentrates, not ongoing day-to-day running. Operate, Deliver, and Support are often grouped together on flashcards but tested separately: Operate means running the service day to day, Deliver means providing the agreed outcomes and value directly to consumers, and Support means resolving the issues and requests that come up once the service is actually in use — distinct jobs that can each go wrong independently of the others.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to the idea of a service lifecycle? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: This maps closely to opening a new restaurant location. Discover is scouting whether there's actual demand in a neighborhood. Design is drawing up the menu and floor plan without ordering a single ingredient yet. Acquire is buying the ovens and dining furniture; Build is training the kitchen staff on the actual recipes in-house. Transition is the soft-opening test run before public launch. And once it's open, Operate is running the kitchen every night, Deliver is the meal actually reaching the table, and Support is handling a customer complaint about a wrong order — three related but genuinely different jobs, exactly like the exam expects you to keep separate.
commonTraps: The eight activities are not a strict one-way pipeline — looping back to an earlier activity, like returning to Design after Build surfaces an issue, is normal and expected.
Design defines requirements only; nothing is actually built or acquired until the activities that follow it.
Operate, Deliver, and Support sound similar but are distinct: running the service, providing the outcome, and resolving issues are three separate jobs.
The value chain and the Product and Service Lifecycle are the same model described two ways, not two separate lists to memorize.
lessons.scenario: A company explores whether customers actually want a self-service password reset tool (Discover), then defines exactly what it needs to do and its security requirements (Design) before writing a single line of code. It buys a third-party identity verification component (Acquire) while its own developers build the reset workflow itself (Build), then runs a controlled pilot with one department before a full release (Transition). Once live, the platform team keeps it running (Operate), users get the actual convenience of resetting their own passwords (Deliver), and the help desk still fields the occasional edge case that fails (Support) — with a spike in failed resets eventually looping the team back to Design to rework the verification flow.
lessons.onTheJob: In practice, the Discover and Design stages are the ones that get skipped under deadline pressure — a team jumps straight to Build because a fix 'obviously' needs writing, and only discovers in Support that nobody actually confirmed the underlying demand was real. The looping-back behavior the framework treats as normal is also what a real change advisory board has to get comfortable with, since a manager who treats a return to Design as a project failure will quietly train their team to hide problems instead of surfacing them.

lessons.title: Value Streams, AI & Adjacent Frameworks
lessons.summary: Mapping how work actually flows, where AI fits into service management, and how ITIL relates to Agile, DevOps, and PRINCE2.
lessons.reading:
A value stream is a series of steps an organization undertakes to create and deliver products and services to consumers, built by combining value chain activities and practices for a specific end-to-end scenario, like "resolve a user's incident," rather than every activity in the lifecycle every time. Value stream mapping visualizes those end-to-end steps specifically to spot waste, delay, or handoffs that don't add value — in practice, this looks like a flowchart with timestamps showing exactly where a request sits waiting versus where real work is actually happening, and it's a diagnostic tool that can be used any time, not only once at project kickoff.

ITIL Version 5 folds AI in as a capability that needs the same governance as anything else, not a special exception. It distinguishes plain AI, systems performing tasks that normally need human intelligence, from generative AI, which creates new content, from agentic AI, which can plan and act autonomously toward a goal with limited human intervention — a chatbot that drafts a reply for a human to approve is generative, while one that files the ticket, checks the knowledge base, and closes it itself is agentic. The AI Capability Model further breaks down what AI actually contributes into six "Cs": Creation, Curation, Clarification, Cognition, Communication, and Coordination — naming which "C" a given AI system performs matters, because a system that curates alerts needs different oversight than one that coordinates automated actions across a workflow.

ITIL deliberately doesn't compete with adjacent frameworks; it operates at a different layer and expects to work alongside them. DevOps contributes specific practices for fast, collaborative delivery — CI/CD pipelines slot naturally inside the Build, Deliver, and Support activities of the lifecycle, governed by ITIL's wider context rather than replacing it. PRINCE2 manages temporary, bounded project work, while ITIL manages the ongoing service that project eventually delivers into — a system rollout might run as a PRINCE2 project, with ITIL practices taking over the moment it goes live. Agile, similarly, is about how work gets done iteratively, while ITIL is about the wider value system that work happens within — different layers, not competing answers to the same question.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to how these frameworks fit together? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Think of ITIL as a restaurant's overall business plan and health-code compliance, while Agile and DevOps are the specific techniques the kitchen uses to cook efficiently, and PRINCE2 is how a one-time kitchen renovation project gets managed. None of them compete with each other — the renovation project (PRINCE2) eventually hands off to day-to-day kitchen operations, governed by the overall plan (ITIL), which might use a fast, iterative prep technique (Agile/DevOps) without that technique ever needing to replace the business plan itself. And an AI system that just suggests tonight's specials based on ingredients about to expire (generative) is a very different level of trust from one that automatically reorders inventory and adjusts the menu on its own (agentic).
commonTraps: Value stream mapping is not a one-time kickoff exercise — it can and should be used whenever waste or delay needs diagnosing.
Agentic AI plans and acts with limited human input; generative AI only produces content on request without that independent follow-through.
PRINCE2 and ITIL are not competing frameworks needing an either/or choice — PRINCE2 manages the bounded project, ITIL manages the ongoing service it feeds into.
AI still needs accountability and risk management like any other capability — governance is not something that only kicks in after something goes wrong.
lessons.scenario: A support team maps its incident-resolution value stream and discovers requests sit untouched in a queue for six hours before anyone even looks at them — the actual troubleshooting itself takes twenty minutes. Around the same time, they roll out an AI system that auto-triages incoming tickets to the right team, an agentic, Coordination-type capability, but require human sign-off before it touches anything on a production database, applying AI governance proportional to risk. The triage rollout itself runs as a short, iterative Agile project, feeding a change into the ongoing service that ITIL governs day to day once it's live.
lessons.onTheJob: Value stream mapping in a real ops team almost always uncovers that the bottleneck isn't the actual technical work but a queue sitting untouched waiting for someone to notice it — the twenty-minutes-of-real-work-versus-six-hours-of-waiting pattern is closer to the norm than the exception. The generative-versus-agentic AI distinction is also what determines who signs off on a rollout in practice: a chatbot that drafts a reply for a human to send gets waved through, while one that can close tickets or touch a production system on its own is where a manager actually has to fight for a governance review before go-live.

cheatSheet.heading: Exam-day strategy
points: You have 60 minutes for 40 questions — about 1.5 minutes each on average. Budget more time for multi-part scenario questions and less for straight recall, rather than pacing every question identically.

Each question is worth one mark and there is no negative marking, so answer every question, even if you have to guess. The pass mark is 65% (26 of 40) — aim comfortably above it rather than for the bare minimum.

Flag anything you're unsure of and move on rather than stalling — a question later in the exam can sometimes jog a detail you needed earlier, and an unanswered question scores nothing, so never run out of time stalling on one.
On multi-select ('choose N') questions, eliminate the options you're confident are wrong first; guessing among 2 plausible answers beats guessing among 4.
Your first read of a question is usually right — change an answer only when you find a specific detail you missed, not from general second-guessing.

cheatSheet.heading: The 7 guiding principles
points: Focus on value — everything traces back to value for stakeholders.
Start where you are — assess and reuse what already exists before building new.
Progress iteratively with feedback — don't try to do everything in one big pass.
Collaborate and promote visibility — work across boundaries, make work visible.
Think and work holistically — no service stands alone.
Keep it simple and practical — use the minimum steps needed.
Optimize and automate — human effort only where it adds real value.

cheatSheet.heading: The 4 dimensions of product and service management
points: Organizations and people — roles, responsibilities, culture, staffing.
Information and technology — the tech and knowledge used to deliver services.
Partners and suppliers — relationships with other organizations involved.
Value streams and processes — the activities, workflows, controls, procedures.

cheatSheet.heading: Product and Service Lifecycle activities
points: Discover → Design → Acquire → Build → Transition → Operate → Deliver → Support.

Eight activities, used iteratively: work can loop back to an earlier activity at any point. This replaces the older six-activity ITIL 4 service value chain (Plan, Improve, Engage, Design & transition, Obtain/build, Deliver & support).
Value streams combine these activities and practices for specific scenarios (e.g. "resolve an incident").

cheatSheet.heading: Key definitions to not mix up
points: Service = a means of enabling value co-creation by facilitating outcomes customers want, without the customer managing costs/risks themselves.
Utility = what the service does (fitness for purpose). Warranty = how well it does it (fitness for use — availability, capacity, security, continuity).
Output = a tangible/intangible deliverable. Outcome = the actual result an output enables for a stakeholder.
Cost and Risk are what value is weighed against — value = (utility + warranty) balanced against cost and risk.

cheatSheet.heading: Practices you must be able to distinguish
points: Incident = unplanned interruption/reduction in quality — restore service fast. Problem = the underlying cause of one or more incidents.
Known Error = a problem that has been analyzed but not yet resolved.
Change Enablement = ensures risks are properly assessed for changes (ITIL uses the term "change enablement" rather than "change management").
Service Request = a formal request for something routine/pre-defined (not an incident — nothing is broken).
Service Level Management = ongoing activity of setting/monitoring/reviewing SLAs, not a one-time contract signing.

cheatSheet.heading: Exam-day reminders
points: Real pass mark: 26/40 (65%), 40 questions, 60 minutes.
Questions often describe a scenario and ask "which practice/principle applies" — map the scenario to the definition, don't just pattern-match keywords.
"Least effort" / "start where you are" language usually points at Start where you are or Keep it simple and practical.

madlibs.scenario: A customer subscribes to a cloud backup service specifically because it does what they need — automatically backing up their files — this 'fitness for purpose' is the service's {b1}. But if that backup service is only available 95% of the time and frequently fails to restore files correctly, its 'fitness for use' — the {b2} — is poor, even though the core function works as designed.

outcome
output
utility
warranty
outcome

madlibs.explanation: Utility is what the service does (functionality); warranty is how well it does it (availability, capacity, security, continuity) — a service can have great utility but poor warranty, or vice versa.

madlibs.scenario: Rather than trying to redesign the entire incident management process in one giant six-month project, the team ships a small improvement, gets feedback, and ships another — following the guiding principle {b1}. When rolling it out, they make sure to involve the service desk agents who'll actually use the new process daily — following {b2}.

madlibs.explanation: "Progress iteratively with feedback" favors small, feedback-driven steps over one big-bang rollout. "Collaborate and promote visibility" is specifically about involving the right stakeholders and being transparent about the work.

madlibs.scenario: When designing a new service, the organization must consider not just its own staff but also the vendors and outsourced providers it depends on — the {b1} dimension. It must also consider the software, hardware, and knowledge/information needed to deliver and support that service — the {b2} dimension.

Partners & Suppliers

Organizations & People

Value Streams & Processes

madlibs.explanation: Partners & Suppliers covers relationships with other organizations involved in service design/delivery/support. Information & Technology covers the technologies and information/knowledge used.

madlibs.scenario: A software company sells a one-time perpetual license for its reporting tool with no ongoing support agreement attached, making it a {b1} rather than a full service provider. Separately, a different client's help desk contract involves the CFO who approved the budget, acting as the {b2}, and the operations manager who defined exactly what the contract needed to cover, acting as the {b3}.

options: digital product vendor
service provider
