madlibs.explanation: A digital product vendor supplies a product, like a perpetual license, without an ongoing service relationship — that's what separates it from a full service provider. The sponsor is whoever authorizes the budget; the customer is whoever defines requirements and is accountable for outcomes — distinct roles, even though one person can sometimes hold more than one of them.

madlibs.scenario: Before a retailer's product team writes a single requirement for a redesigned self-checkout kiosk, they spend two weeks observing store staff and interviewing customers to understand exactly where the current kiosk frustrates people — that exploratory activity is {b1}. Once they've translated those findings into concrete functional and security specifications for the fix, the work moves into {b2}. Only once the updated kiosk software has been tested and is being rolled out into live stores does the work reach {b3}.

madlibs.explanation: Discover is about understanding demand and opportunity before anything is specified — exactly the observation-and-interview work described. Design is where requirements and specifications get defined, but nothing is built yet. Transition is specifically where a new or changed product moves into live use, including testing and release, which is what rolling the kiosk update out to stores actually is.

madlibs.scenario: A service desk's virtual agent drafts a suggested reply to a routine password-reset ticket, which a human agent reviews and sends — under the AI Capability Model, that's an example of AI performing {b1}. Later, the team adds a feature that automatically reads every incoming support email and files it into the correct queue with no human involved at any point — that's an example of {b2} instead.

options: Creation
Curation
Cognition
Coordination
Creation
Curation
Cognition
Coordination

madlibs.explanation: Creation covers AI generating new content, like a drafted reply — even though a human still reviews it before it goes out. Curation covers organizing and filtering information, which is exactly what auto-sorting incoming emails into the right queue is; it isn't generating new content, so it doesn't count as Creation, and there's no decision-making or orchestration of a broader workflow involved, which is what Cognition and Coordination would describe.

sequences.prompt: Put these steps in order according to ITIL's Continual Improvement Model.
steps: Where do we want to be?
How do we keep the momentum going?
sequences.explanation: The Continual Improvement Model always starts with the big-picture vision, then assesses the current and desired states before planning and acting — assessing results and sustaining momentum only make sense once action has actually been taken.

sequences.prompt: Put these steps in order for handling a P1 incident per ITIL practice.
steps: Escalate to the appropriate resolver group if needed
Close the incident once the user confirms resolution
sequences.explanation: An incident has to be logged before it can be categorized/prioritized at all, and escalation happens during diagnosis when the first-line team can't resolve it alone — closure is always last, and specifically requires the user's confirmation, not just the fix being technically applied.

sequences.prompt: Put these steps in order for a normal change going through ITIL change enablement.
steps: Submit a change request describing what and why
Assess the risk and impact of the proposed change
Obtain authorization from the change authority
Review the change afterward to confirm it achieved its objective
sequences.explanation: Risk/impact assessment has to happen before authorization can be meaningfully granted — an authority approving blind, unassessed risk defeats the point of change enablement. The post-implementation review is what actually closes the loop on whether the change worked.

caseStudies.title: Northwind Logistics' Struggling Service Desk
caseStudies.scenario: Northwind Logistics runs a 24-person service desk supporting 3,000 warehouse and office staff. Over the last quarter, the same barcode-scanner connectivity issue has been logged as a fresh incident more than 40 times; agents keep applying the same workaround (a device reboot and a Wi-Fi profile reset) without ever recording why the underlying fault happens. Meanwhile, the desk's manager has noticed that when a new hire is added to a distribution team, requests for a laptop, a badge, and system access are handled as three separate, uncoordinated tickets routed to three different teams, each unaware of the others' status. Leadership also wants smaller, faster improvements to the ticketing workflow rather than a single, disruptive process overhaul, and wants the team that actually works the desk each day involved in shaping any changes, not just told about them after the fact.

questions.question: Which ITIL practice is missing from how the recurring barcode-scanner issue is being handled, given that the same workaround is applied over and over without ever recording why?
options: Problem management
Incident management
Change enablement
Service request management
questions.explanation: Problem management is specifically about identifying and recording the underlying cause of recurring incidents (a known error) so a permanent fix, not just a repeated workaround, becomes possible. Incident management is what's already happening every time the desk logs and resolves the issue in the moment; change enablement and service request management don't address root-cause investigation at all.

questions.question: True or false: routing a new hire's laptop, badge, and access requests as three separate, uncoordinated tickets is a well-designed value stream for onboarding.
questions.explanation: A value stream is the end-to-end series of steps that should deliver a specific outcome — here, a fully onboarded new hire — as one coordinated flow. Three teams working in isolation, each unaware of the others' status, is exactly the kind of disconnected handoff that value stream mapping exists to expose and fix, not a sign of good design.

questions.question: Leadership wants smaller, faster improvements to the ticketing workflow instead of one disruptive overhaul, and wants the agents who work the desk daily involved in shaping the changes. Which pair of ITIL guiding principles does this describe?
options: Progress iteratively with feedback, and Collaborate and promote visibility
Keep it simple and practical, and Optimize and automate
Focus on value, and Think and work holistically
Start where you are, and Focus on value
questions.explanation: "Progress iteratively with feedback" is exactly about favoring small, feedback-driven steps over one big-bang overhaul. "Collaborate and promote visibility" is specifically about involving the people who'll actually do the work in shaping it, and being transparent with them, rather than deciding changes in isolation and announcing them afterward.
questions.whyTested: The scenario names no principle directly — it only describes behavior (small steps, involving the desk staff). The exam is testing whether you can map described behavior back to the correct named principle, instead of just recognizing the principle's name when it's already given to you.

questions.question: Once problem management identifies the barcode-scanner fault's underlying cause but no permanent fix is available yet, which of the following would be appropriate next steps? (Select all that apply.)
options: Record it as a known error, with the existing workaround documented for agents to apply consistently
Close problem management's involvement immediately, since incident management can keep handling it case by case
Raise a change request to implement a permanent fix once one is identified
Stop logging future occurrences as incidents, since the cause is now understood
questions.explanation: A known error is precisely a problem that has been analyzed but not yet permanently resolved, with a workaround recorded so it can be applied consistently rather than reinvented each time. A permanent fix still requires a proper change request to be assessed, authorized, and implemented. Problem management shouldn't simply hand back to incident management and disengage, and each new occurrence is still a real incident affecting a user — it still needs to be logged, even though its underlying cause is now known.

compare.scenario: A client's finance lead says the new expense tool 'works perfectly', yet month-end close still takes a week because approvals pile up with one manager. The provider asks how to frame the improvement. Which framing is more correct?
compare.optionA: An outcome gap: the output, a working tool, was delivered, but the outcome of a faster close was not, so the approval flow is where to look.
compare.optionB: A warranty gap: the tool is not performing to the client's needs, so the availability and capacity targets should be reviewed.
compare.why: The tool does what it should and is available when needed, so utility and warranty are both fine. What is missing is the result the client wanted, which makes this an output-versus-outcome problem. The warranty framing is tempting because the client is dissatisfied, but warranty covers availability, capacity, security, and continuity, and none of those is failing here.

compare.scenario: An MSP wants to change the response-time targets in a support contract. The client's CFO funds the contract; the client's head of operations defined the targets and reports against them. Whom should the MSP treat as the decision-maker on the targets themselves?
compare.optionA: The CFO, as sponsor, because any change to targets alters what the budget is buying.
compare.optionB: The head of operations, as customer, because the customer defines requirements and is accountable for the outcomes.
compare.why: Response-time targets are requirements, and defining requirements is the customer role, so the head of operations decides what the targets should be. The sponsor framing is not wrong, since the CFO must agree any change that affects cost, but it answers who authorizes the spend rather than who owns the requirement, which is what the question asks.

compare.scenario: A hospital licenses a scheduling tool from a software firm and pays an MSP to run it. A vendor patch breaks a feature, and the hospital's director asks who owns restoring the service for the hospital. Which answer is more correct?
compare.optionA: The software firm, as the digital product vendor, because the defect is in its product.
compare.optionB: The MSP, as the service provider, because it holds the service relationship with the hospital even though it depends on the vendor for the fix.
compare.why: The hospital's service relationship is with the MSP, so the MSP owns restoring service and managing the vendor to get the fix. The vendor answer correctly locates the defect, but a digital product vendor supplies a product without a service relationship to the consumer, so it is not accountable to the hospital for the outcome. Where the bug lives and who owns the service are different questions.

compare.scenario: Checkout fails at 09:00 on the third Monday in a row. Each time, restarting one service fixes it within ten minutes. The ops lead has thirty free minutes today. Which use of that time better reflects ITIL practice?
compare.optionA: Document the restart as a standard change so next Monday's fix is pre-authorized and even faster.
compare.optionB: Open a problem record and start investigating why the service fails every Monday morning.
compare.why: Three identical incidents point to an underlying cause, and investigating causes to prevent recurrence is problem management. Pre-authorizing the restart is a sensible refinement of the workaround and may still be worth doing, but it optimizes how fast the symptom is cleared while leaving the Monday failure in place, which is the incident-versus-problem distinction the exam tests.

compare.scenario: A monthly OS patch has been applied as a pre-authorized standard change for two years. This month the vendor flags the patch as high impact because it rewrites the kernel scheduler. How should the team handle it?
compare.optionA: Apply it as a standard change as usual, since the standard-change authorization was granted for this patch cycle.
compare.optionB: Treat this month's patch as a normal change, since the pre-authorization assumed a low-risk, well-understood change and this one is neither.
compare.why: A standard change is pre-authorized because it is low risk and well understood; when a specific instance stops meeting that description, it needs assessment and authorization, which is a normal change. Following the existing authorization is procedurally defensible, but it treats the label as permanent when the classification was always conditional on the risk profile.

compare.scenario: A user emails the desk: 'My laptop is fine, but I need Visio installed by Thursday for a client workshop.' The analyst has to log it. Which classification is more correct?
compare.optionA: A service request, because nothing is broken and software installation is a routine, pre-defined request.
compare.optionB: An incident, because the user cannot do the workshop without Visio and the deadline makes it urgent.
compare.why: An incident is an unplanned interruption or reduction in service quality, and the user says nothing is broken. Urgency and a deadline affect priority, not classification, so a time-critical request is still a service request. The incident framing feels responsive, but misclassifying requests as incidents distorts incident metrics and bypasses the fulfilment path designed for this work.

compare.scenario: A CIO is alarmed by change-related outages and wants to intervene at the right level. Which action better reflects the governance role, as opposed to stepping into day-to-day management?
compare.optionA: Set a policy that every change must carry a documented risk assessment, then review compliance and outage trends each quarter.
compare.optionB: Join the weekly change advisory board personally so that no risky change is approved without her sign-off.
compare.why: Governance is evaluating, directing, and monitoring: setting the rule and checking it is followed. Sitting on the board puts the CIO inside the change enablement practice, approving individual changes, which is management work rather than governance. It might reduce risk in the short term, but it does not create the direction and oversight that keep working when she is not in the room.

compare.scenario: A team wants to cut incident resolution time. They have a vision statement and leadership support but no current measurements. A consultant offers two next steps. Which is more correct under the Continual Improvement Model?
compare.optionA: Spend two weeks measuring current resolution times by category before setting any target.
compare.optionB: Set a stretch target of 50% faster now to create urgency, then measure progress against it.
compare.why: The model's steps depend on each other: 'where do we want to be?' only makes sense after 'where are we now?' has produced an honest baseline. Setting a target first does create urgency, which is why it is tempting, but a 50% figure chosen without a baseline is a guess, and the team will have no way to tell later whether they got there.

compare.scenario: A company outsources its service desk. The HR director asks which of the four dimensions the retraining of the remaining in-house staff falls under. Which answer is more correct?
compare.optionA: Partners and suppliers, because the retraining is a direct consequence of the new outsourcing relationship.
compare.optionB: Organizations and people, because the change concerns the skills and roles of the company's own staff, whatever triggered it.
compare.why: Dimensions are assigned by what is changing, not by what caused the change. Skills and roles of staff are organizations and people; the outsourcing contract itself is partners and suppliers. The outsourcing-driven answer correctly traces the cause but then files the effect under it, which is how a single change ends up wrongly treated as touching only one dimension.

compare.scenario: A pilot with one department has run for a month. The platform team patches the tool weekly and the help desk fixes login issues as they arise, but the tool has not been offered to other departments. Which description of where the work sits is more correct?
compare.optionA: Transition: the service is still being moved into full live use, even though operate- and support-type work is already happening for the pilot group.
compare.optionB: Operate: patching and fixing issues means the service is live, so the lifecycle has moved past Transition.
compare.why: A pilot is a controlled release, which is Transition work, and the service as a whole has not yet reached live use for its intended consumers. The Operate answer is understandable because operate and support activities are genuinely happening for the pilot users, but the lifecycle is iterative and activities overlap; the presence of patching does not mean the release itself is finished.

compare.scenario: A manager wants to speed up employee onboarding. Access provisioning is the slowest single step measured so far, but nobody has looked at the whole flow. Which first move is more correct?
compare.optionA: Tighten the access team's internal target first, since provisioning is the slowest step measured so far.
compare.optionB: Map the onboarding value stream end to end, from signed offer to productive first day, before changing any single team's target.
compare.why: Onboarding is a value stream spanning several teams, and the delay most often sits in the handoffs and queues between steps rather than inside the step that happens to have been measured. Tightening one team's target is a reasonable practice-level fix, but without the end-to-end map it may simply move the wait to the next handoff while the new starter's first productive day does not change.

compare.scenario: A desk pilots an AI assistant that proposes a category for each new ticket; analysts accept or change the suggestion. The manager asks what level of governance is proportionate. Which answer is more correct?
compare.optionA: Assign an owner, monitor acceptance and override rates, and review quarterly, since a human confirms every suggestion.
compare.optionB: Route each new suggestion pattern through the change authority before analysts may act on it, since AI is involved.
compare.why: ITIL applies AI governance in proportion to risk. With a human confirming every suggestion, the exposure is low, so clear ownership plus monitoring and periodic review is sufficient and still proactive. Routing every pattern through the change authority is governance applied by category rather than by risk; it would add delay without reducing a risk that the human-in-the-loop design already controls.
